quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the parts of a Bedford cord: cords, cutting ends, stuffer ends and the floats that shape them.

questions.q: In which direction do the ribs of a Bedford cord run?
options: Weft-way, across the cloth
Warp-way, along the cloth
Diagonally, like a twill line
In both directions, forming a check
questions.explain: Bedford cord shows rounded warp-way ribs; each cord is a group of ends. Weft-way cords are the piqué family, treated in the next lecture.

questions.q: What are the cutting ends in a Bedford cord?
options: A pair of ends between the cords that weave plain with every pick
Coarse ends lying straight inside each cord
Ends that are cut away after weaving to separate the cords
The twill-face ends that are cropped in finishing
questions.explain: The cutting ends weave plain on every pick, so they interlace tightly and make the sunk line between cords. Nothing is cut; the name describes the sharp line they create.

questions.q: What is the purpose of stuffer ends?
options: To make the sunk line between cords deeper
To hold the weft floats on the back in place
To lie straight inside the cord and make it fuller and rounder
To change the face weave from plain to twill
questions.explain: Stuffer ends are coarse ends lying straight between the face and the back floats; they fill the cord so it looks rounder. They do not interlace, so they neither sink the line nor change the face weave.

questions.q: In a Bedford cord the long weft floats that form the ridges lie on the face of the cloth.
questions.explain: The floats are on the back, under the cord that is not weaving on that pick. It is their pull from behind that raises the cord into a ridge; the face shows only plain or twill.

questions.q: What actually pulls each cord up into a rounded ridge?
options: The high tension of the cutting ends
The twill diagonal of the face weave
The stuffer ends being lifted on every pick
The loose weft floats on the back of the cord
questions.explain: The lecture states that the floats on the back pull each cord into a ridge. Stuffer ends only fill the ridge; the cutting ends define its edges.

questions.q: Which weaves may form the face of a Bedford cord in this lecture?
options: Satin or sateen only
Plain or twill
Honeycomb or huckaback
Only a 2/2 hopsack
questions.explain: The lecture gives a plain-face cord (24 ends × 4 picks) and a twill-face cord whose face is a 2/1 twill (22 ends × 6 picks).

questions.q: The cutting ends are lifted on alternate picks, that is, they interlace plain with every pick.
questions.explain: A pair of cutting ends weaves plain with every pick; one end is up and the other down, swapping on each pick. That constant interlacing makes the sunk line.

questions.q: On a pick that weaves plain with cord A, what does the weft do under cord B?
options: It floats loosely under all the ends of cord B
It also weaves plain with cord B
It weaves 2/1 twill with cord B
It is cut and does not reach cord B
questions.explain: On each pick the weft weaves with one cord and floats under the other; the next pick reverses the roles. That alternation is the whole principle of the structure.

questions.q: In the twill-face example of the lecture, which weave forms the face of the cords?
options: 3/1 twill
2/2 twill
2/1 twill
1/2 twill
questions.explain: The twill-face Bedford cord in the lecture has a 2/1 twill face, which is why six picks (two cords × three-pick twill) complete the repeat.

questions.q: The two-colour cord effect described in the lecture is produced by colouring the picks, not by using two differently coloured warps.
questions.explain: Weaving the two pick-pairs in red and green gives each cord a solid colour because only its own weaving picks show on its face; the warp is a single colour.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How the repeat size, number of healds and float length follow from the face weave and the pick order.

questions.q: Why does the plain-face Bedford cord repeat on 4 picks?
options: Because there are four cutting ends
Because each cord needs two plain-weave picks and the two cords weave alternately
Because the draft uses four healds for the cords
Because the stuffer ends need four picks to lie straight
questions.explain: Plain weave needs 2 picks per cord; two cords weaving in turn gives 2 × 2 = 4 picks. The number of healds and cutting ends has no bearing on the pick repeat.

questions.q: A Bedford cord with a 2/1 twill face repeats on how many picks?
questions.explain: The 2/1 twill needs 3 picks on each cord and the two cords weave in turn, so 3 × 2 = 6 picks. A 3-pick answer forgets the second cord.

questions.q: A Bedford cord has a 3/1 twill face and the picks alternate singly between the two cords. How many picks make one repeat?
questions.explain: A 3/1 twill repeats on 4 picks; each of the two cords needs its own 4 weaving picks, so the repeat is 4 × 2 = 8 picks.

questions.q: How many healds does the 24-end plain-face Bedford cord need, and why?
options: 6: two for the cutting ends and two for each cord
24: one for every end in the repeat
4: two for cutting ends and two for both cords together
8: four for each cord
questions.explain: Threading 1 2 3 4 3 4 … 1 2 5 6 5 6 … uses healds 1–2 for cutting ends, 3–4 for cord A and 5–6 for cord B. Cord B cannot share cord A's healds because it lifts on the opposite picks.

questions.q: If each cord of a plain-face Bedford cord is made wider by adding more ends, what happens to the number of healds required?
options: It rises by one heald per extra end
It doubles
It rises by two healds per cord
It stays the same
questions.explain: Extra cord ends are simply threaded alternately on the same two healds of that cord, so the heald count is unchanged; only the lifting plan's repeat in ends grows.

questions.q: Changing the plain-face cord from 1-and-1 to 2-and-2 pick order changes which of the following?
options: The number of picks in the repeat
The number of healds
The order in which weaving and floating picks occur
The number of cutting ends
questions.explain: In 2-and-2 order two consecutive picks weave cord A while floating under cord B, then two do the reverse. The repeat is still 24 ends × 4 picks and the draft is unchanged.

questions.q: Stuffer ends are lifted on the picks that float under their cord and lowered on the picks that weave with it.
questions.explain: That is exactly how the lecture describes them: lifted on the floating picks, lowered on the weaving picks, so they lie straight between the face weft and the back floats.

questions.q: The stuffer version of the plain-face cord has 28 ends instead of 24. How many stuffer ends sit in each cord?
questions.explain: 28 − 24 = 4 extra ends shared between two cords, so 2 stuffer ends per cord, placed in the middle of each cord.

questions.q: In the 24-end plain-face cord (2 cutting + 10 cord + 2 cutting + 10 cord ends), how many ends does each weft float on the back pass under?
options: 10 ends
12 ends
24 ends
5 ends
questions.explain: On a floating pick all 10 ends of the non-weaving cord are lifted, so the weft floats under 10 ends. The cutting ends on either side still interlace, so the float cannot be 12.

questions.q: To obtain a red cord next to a green cord from one single-colour warp, what must be arranged?
options: Alternate red and green ends across each cord
Weave the cutting ends in red and the stuffers in green
Use a red face warp and a green stitching warp
Insert the picks that weave cord A in red and those that weave cord B in green
questions.explain: Each cord shows only its own weaving picks on its face, so colouring the two pick groups differently colours the two cords differently. The warp stays one colour.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting ends, healds, floats and repeats from the Bedford cord drafts in the lecture.

questions.q: The threading order is 1 2 3 4 3 4 3 4 3 4 3 4 1 2 5 6 5 6 5 6 5 6 5 6. How many ends are drawn on heald 3?
questions.explain: Ends 3–12 (10 ends) alternate on healds 3 and 4, so heald 3 carries 10 ÷ 2 = 5 ends.

questions.q: In the same 24-end threading, how many ends in total are drawn on healds 1 and 2 together?
questions.explain: Both pairs of cutting ends (ends 1–2 and 13–14) use healds 1 and 2, so 2 + 2 = 4 ends.

questions.q: A twill-face Bedford cord has 2 cutting ends, a cord of 9 ends, 2 more cutting ends and a second cord of 9 ends. How many ends are in the repeat?
questions.explain: 2 + 9 + 2 + 9 = 22 ends, which is the lecture's 22-end twill-face example.

questions.q: The plain-face design is 24 ends × 4 picks. How many point-paper squares does one repeat occupy?
questions.explain: Ends × picks = 24 × 4 = 96 squares in one repeat of the design.

questions.q: The stuffer-end version is 28 ends × 4 picks and the fabric effect is drawn at 2× repeat. How many ends are shown across the drawing?
questions.explain: Two repeats of 28 ends = 56 ends across.

questions.q: A 2/1 twill-face Bedford cord is drafted with 2 healds for the cutting ends and a separate straight draft of 3 healds for each cord. How many healds in all?
questions.explain: 2 (cutting) + 3 (cord A, 2/1 twill) + 3 (cord B) = 8 healds. Cord B needs its own healds because it lifts on different picks from cord A.

questions.q: A cloth is woven at 60 ends per inch with the 24-end plain-face repeat, which contains two cords. How many cords are there per inch?
questions.explain: Repeats per inch = 60 ÷ 24 = 2.5; each repeat holds two cords, so 2.5 × 2 = 5 cords per inch.

questions.q: A weft float passes under a cord of 10 ends in a cloth set at 50 ends per inch. What is the float length in inches (to two decimals)?
questions.explain: 10 ends ÷ 50 ends per inch = 0.20 inch for each back float.

questions.q: On a weaving pick the first four ends are: cutting end 1 up, cutting end 2 down, cord end 3 up, cord end 4 down. Taking 1 = up and the first end as the most significant bit, which hex digit encodes this group?
options: $A
$C
questions.explain: Up-down-up-down is 1010 in binary, which is hex $A. $5 (0101) would be the same picture with the lifts reversed, $C is 1100 and $3 is 0011.

questions.q: In the 24-end draft, the ten ends of cord B are threaded alternately on healds 5 and 6.
questions.explain: The threading ends with 5 6 5 6 5 6 5 6 5 6: ten ends alternating on healds 5 and 6 form cord B.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions a designer or weaving manager makes when a Bedford cord is sampled, costed or goes wrong on the loom.

questions.q: A buyer asks for fuller, rounder cords than your sample shows. What is the standard structural remedy?
options: Add more cutting ends between the cords
Change the plain face to a twill face
Add coarse stuffer ends in the middle of each cord
Reduce the picks per inch
questions.explain: Stuffer ends lie straight inside the cord and pad it out. More cutting ends only widen the sunk line and a twill face changes surface, not fullness.

questions.q: A sample shows cords that look flat with hardly any ridge. Which is the most likely structural cause?
options: Too many cutting ends
The weft floats on the back are too short or too slack to pull the cords up
Too few healds were used
The twill runs in the wrong direction
questions.explain: It is the back floats that pull the cords into ridges; if they are very short (narrow cords) or inserted slack they cannot draw the face up. Heald count and twill direction do not affect the relief.

questions.q: A mill has a tappet loom limited to 6 healds. Which of the lecture's designs can it weave with a straight draft per cord?
options: The 24-end plain-face cord
The 22-end 2/1 twill-face cord
Both of them
Neither of them
questions.explain: The plain-face cord needs 6 healds (2 + 2 + 2). The twill-face cord needs 2 + 3 + 3 = 8 healds, beyond the loom's capacity.

questions.q: The sales office wants the two cords in different colours without a second warp beam. What do you change?
options: Dye the cutting ends a second colour
Thread alternate cords from differently coloured cones at warping
Add coloured stuffer ends
Weave the picks for cord A in one colour and the picks for cord B in another
questions.explain: Each cord shows only its own weaving picks, so a two-colour weft colours the cords separately. Warping alternate cords in two colours would also work, but the question asks for the lecture's single-warp method using the weft.

questions.q: A Bedford cord with a 2/1 twill face can be woven on a loom with only six healds.
questions.explain: Each cord needs three healds for its 2/1 twill and the cutting ends need two more, giving eight. Six healds suffice only for the plain-face version.

questions.q: In a trial cloth the sunk line between cords has disappeared and adjacent cords merge. What was probably done wrong on the peg plan?
options: The stuffer ends were lowered on the weaving picks
The cutting ends were lifted with their neighbouring cord instead of weaving plain on every pick
The weft floated on two picks instead of one
The two cords were given different widths
questions.explain: The sunk line exists only because the cutting ends interlace plain on every pick. If they follow a cord's lifts they float with it and the dividing line vanishes.

questions.q: Which yarn is the most sensible choice for stuffer ends?
options: A fine, highly twisted yarn of the same count as the face
A yarn dyed to match the weft exactly
A coarse yarn, since it only has to fill the cord and is hidden inside it
A sized, high-tension yarn like a stitching warp
questions.explain: Stuffers lie straight and are hidden, so a coarse (and possibly cheaper) yarn gives the most fullness for the cost; colour and fine twist are wasted on them.

questions.q: Why are stuffer ends in practice often wound on a separate beam from the face warp?
options: They lie straight without interlacing, so they take up less length than the face ends
They must be sized with a different size recipe
They are coloured and would stain the face warp
They are lifted on every pick
questions.explain: Interlacing face ends take up more length per metre of cloth than straight stuffers; one beam would let the stuffers go slack, so a second beam (or separate tensioning) is used.

questions.q: Making each cord narrower (fewer ends per cord) shortens the weft floats on the back.
questions.explain: Each back float passes under all the ends of one cord, so float length equals cord width in ends; fewer ends means a shorter float.

questions.q: A designer wants cord A with a plain face (4-pick repeat for the pair of cords) and cord B with a 2/1 twill face (6-pick repeat) in the same cloth. On how many picks must the combined design repeat?
questions.explain: The two orders of weaving must come back into step together, so the repeat is the least common multiple of 4 and 6, which is 12 picks.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the whole lecture, including the mistakes students most often make when drawing Bedford cords.

questions.q: In the stuffer-end version, where does a stuffer end lie relative to the weft?
options: Above all the weft, on the face of the cord
Between the face weft and the back float of its own cord
Below all the weft, on the back of the cloth
Interlaced plain with every pick
questions.explain: Lowered on weaving picks (face weft above it) and lifted on floating picks (back float below it), the stuffer is sandwiched inside the cord and never shows.

questions.q: A student draws the cutting ends so that they float with cord A on the floating picks and interlace only on cord A's weaving picks. What will the cloth show?
options: A deeper sunk line
Cords of two different widths
A twill line across the cords
No clear line between the cords, because the cutting ends no longer interlace on every pick
questions.explain: The sunk line depends on the cutting ends weaving plain with every pick; letting them float with a cord removes the dividing line and the cords run together.

questions.q: A plain-face Bedford cord repeat has 2 cutting ends, a cord of 14 ends containing 2 stuffer ends, then 2 cutting ends and a second cord of 14 ends also containing 2 stuffer ends. How many ends are in the repeat?
questions.explain: The stuffers are already counted within each 14-end cord, so 2 + 14 + 2 + 14 = 32 ends. Adding the stuffers again (36) is the common double-counting error.

questions.q: A cloth woven at 72 ends per inch uses the 28-end stuffer repeat. How many repeats fit across a 60-inch warp width? Give the answer to one decimal place.
questions.explain: Total ends = 72 × 60 = 4,320; 4,320 ÷ 28 = 154.3 repeats across the width.

questions.q: In the 22-end twill-face cord each cord has 9 ends rather than 10. Why?
options: 9 is a multiple of 3, the end repeat of the 2/1 twill face
The twill needs an odd number of ends to show a diagonal
The cutting ends take one end from each cord
9 ends give the same float length as 10
questions.explain: A 2/1 twill repeats on 3 ends, so each cord should contain whole twill repeats: 9 = 3 × 3. A 10-end cord would break the twill at its edge.

questions.q: In the 24-end draft, cutting ends 13–14 share healds 1 and 2 with ends 1–2 because both pairs lift in exactly the same way on every pick.
questions.explain: All cutting ends weave plain on every pick, so their lifts are identical and a single pair of healds serves both pairs.

questions.q: The picks are inserted red, green, red, green in 1-and-1 order and cord A weaves on the odd picks. What colour does cord A show?
options: Green
Red and green mixed
Red
Neither: the warp colour hides the weft
questions.explain: Odd picks are red and only cord A's own weaving picks show on its face, so cord A is solid red and cord B solid green.

questions.q: Which statement about the back of a Bedford cord is correct?
options: It is identical to the face
It shows loose weft floats under each cord in turn
It shows the stuffer ends weaving plain
It shows long warp floats
questions.explain: Under each cord the weft floats on the picks it is not weaving with, so the back carries loose weft floats; the stuffers are hidden inside and there are no warp floats.

questions.q: A plain-face Bedford cord repeats on 4 picks and the cloth has 24 picks per cm. What is the length of one repeat in the weft direction, in mm (to two decimals)?
questions.explain: 4 picks ÷ 24 picks per cm = 0.1667 cm = 1.67 mm per repeat.

questions.q: A student claims that the 1-and-1 pick order gives back floats twice as long as the 2-and-2 order. What is the correct view?
options: Correct: alternating picks double the float
Correct, but only on the twill-face version
Wrong: 2-and-2 order doubles the float, not 1-and-1
Wrong: float length is set by the width of the cord, not by the pick order
questions.explain: Each float passes under all the ends of one cord whatever the pick order. 2-and-2 merely puts two such floats on consecutive picks; it does not lengthen them.
